issues.legal_issue: A quasi-permanent allotment of evacuee agricultural land did not constitute property attracting the constitutional protections claimed.
material_facts: The applicants held agricultural land under quasi-permanent allotments made to displaced landholders.
The allotments conferred use and occupation, including rights that could benefit heirs, but the original owners retained ultimate ownership while the land remained evacuee property.
The allotments were subject to statutory cancellation or resumption powers, and the applicants could not ordinarily transfer them by sale, mortgage, gift, or will.
The applicants had not received instruments transferring permanent ownership of the allotted land.
issues.conclusion: The interest created by a quasi-permanent allotment was not property attracting protection under Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1), or 31(2) of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1), 31(2), and 31(2A), and the statutory scheme under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, including sections 8–10, 12, and 16; the 1949 allotment conditions; the relevant rules governing cancellation; and sections 10, 12, and 19 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, together with rules 72(2) and 102. The statutory grant remained provisional and subject to cancellation; it was not transferable or disposable in the ordinary ways required for protection under Article 19(1)(f), and it did not amount to ownership or a right of possession of the kind addressed by Article 31(2). The Court distinguished the stage at which permanent ownership was granted by a sanad. It noted Dunichand Hakim v. Deputy Commissioner as background to the rehabilitation scheme, and disagreed with the view in Suraj Parkash Kapur v. State of Punjab insofar as it treated the allottee’s interest as constitutionally protected property.

rule.if: constitutional_petition_challenging_allotment_cancellation and statutory_use_and_occupation_grant and (grantor_retains_cancellation_power and interest_is_not_ordinarily_transferable) and (ultimate_title_remains_with_original_owner or permanent_title_instrument_not_issued)

predicates.constitutional_petition_challenging_allo: A person sought constitutional relief against cancellation of an allotment of land.
predicates.statutory_use_and_occupation_grant: An authority granted a person use and occupation of land under a statutory allotment scheme.
predicates.grantor_retains_cancellation_power: The authority granting the allotment retained power to cancel or resume it.
predicates.interest_is_not_ordinarily_transferable: The allottee could not ordinarily transfer or dispose of the interest in the land.
predicates.ultimate_title_remains_with_original_own: The original owner retained ultimate title to the land while it remained within the scheme.
predicates.permanent_title_instrument_not_issued: The allottee had not received an instrument granting permanent ownership.

issues.definition: When a constitutional petition challenges cancellation of a statutory use-and-occupation allotment that remains provisional, cancellable, and without permanent title, the allotment interest is not constitutionally protected property.

issues.legal_issue: Cancellation of the allotment did not deprive the applicants of property without authority of law.
material_facts: The allotments were subject to powers of cancellation under the governing law and rules.
The cancellation was made by the responsible authorities as part of a readjustment of land allotments following a higher authority’s direction.
The applicants sought revision, and the reviewing authority heard them before dismissing their challenge.
The cancellation was an exercise of the statutory power governing the allotments, not an usurpation of jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming that the allotment interest was property, its cancellation was not a deprivation without authority of law and did not infringe a fundamental right.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(1) requires both deprivation of property and deprivation without authority of law. The Court applied section 12 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, and the rules governing cancellation, including the 1949 allotment conditions and the applicable rules made under the Act. Sections 28 and 46 of the Act made the relevant orders final and barred civil or revenue court challenges to matters entrusted to the authorities. The Court noted the broader view expressed in State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose about deprivation of an individual right within a bundle of property rights, but observed that the other members of the Court had not shared that view; it held that, in any event, the cancellation here was authorized by law. The principle in Julius v. Lord Bishop of Oxford did not establish an indefeasible entitlement to transfer of the allotted land because the allotment remained subject to cancellation under the applicable statutory scheme.

predicates.constitutional_petition_challenging_allo: A person sought constitutional relief against cancellation of an allotment of land.
predicates.allotment_rights_are_subject_to_statutor: The allottee's rights were expressly subject to cancellation under the governing scheme.
predicates.cancellation_is_made_by_authorized_offic: An official responsible for administering the allotment scheme cancelled the allotment.
predicates.under_statutory_power: The official relied on a legal power governing cancellation of the allotment.
predicates.order_is_within_authority_jurisdiction: The cancellation was an exercise of the authority's assigned function rather than an usurpation of jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When an authorized official cancels a legally cancellable allotment within the official's assigned authority, that cancellation is not deprivation without authority of law.
